scope: Classroom-facing learning content for a safe virtual demo. It explains classroom-relevant materials, concepts and reference entries only. The software does not provide procedures for unsafe real-world chemistry.

materials.name: Water
materials.concept: A polar molecular compound and the most common classroom solvent.
materials.explanation: Water molecules are polar, which helps explain why water can surround and disperse many ionic and polar particles.
learning_goals: Distinguish a compound from an element.
Identify solvent and solute in a solution.
Connect molecular polarity to solution formation.
observations: Water is the solvent phase in the model.
The model can show water temperature, but it does not yet provide a complete evaporation and condensation cycle.

materials.name: Sodium chloride (table salt)
materials.concept: An ionic compound made of sodium and chloride ions in a repeating crystal lattice.
materials.explanation: When sodium chloride dissolves, water molecules interact with the ions and disperse them through the liquid.
learning_goals: Recognize an ionic compound.
Explain dissolution as particle separation and solvation.
Distinguish a solution from a visible solid mixture.
observations: The virtual model shows the solid gradually becoming distributed through the water.
The solution remains visually clear in this model.

materials.name: Ice
materials.explanation: Ice is useful for teaching state changes because it can melt back into liquid water when energy is added.
learning_goals: Identify the solid state of a familiar substance.
Describe melting as a physical change.
Relate state changes to energy transfer.
observations: Reference entry only; not part of the classroom demo setup by default.

materials.name: Sand
materials.concept: An insoluble granular material used for mixture and separation lessons.
materials.explanation: Sand does not dissolve in water, so it is useful for discussing heterogeneous mixtures and separation ideas.
learning_goals: Distinguish soluble and insoluble materials.
Recognize a heterogeneous mixture.
Explain why filtration can separate suspended solids from liquids.
observations: Reference entry only; it is not a teaching reagent in the default classroom demo.

materials.name: Air
materials.concept: A mixture of gases used to discuss the gaseous state and gas exchange.
materials.explanation: Air is not a single compound. It is a mixture mainly containing nitrogen and oxygen.
learning_goals: Recognize that some everyday substances are mixtures rather than compounds.
Describe the gaseous state as a particle-level model.
Discuss why gases fill the available space.
observations: Reference entry only; it is used for conceptual discussion rather than as a playable reagent.

materials.name: Carbon dioxide
materials.concept: A gaseous molecular compound produced and used in many biological and Earth-system processes.
materials.explanation: Carbon dioxide is useful for teaching because it appears in biology, respiration, photosynthesis and Earth science.
learning_goals: Read a molecular formula.
Connect chemistry ideas to life science and Earth science.
Describe a gas at the particle level.
observations: Reference entry only; it is not a default playable reagent.

materials.name: Glucose
materials.concept: A simple sugar and an important biological energy molecule.
materials.explanation: Glucose is a molecular compound containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
learning_goals: Read a molecular formula.
Distinguish molecular compounds from ionic compounds.
Recognize glucose as a biologically important fuel molecule.
observations: Reference entry only; it is not part of the classroom demonstration setup.

materials.name: Sucrose
materials.concept: A molecular carbohydrate commonly known as table sugar.
materials.explanation: Sucrose molecules can become dispersed among water molecules without changing into different substances.
learning_goals: Compare molecular and ionic solutes.
Understand a homogeneous solution at the particle level.
observations: Reference entry only; it is not part of the classroom demonstration setup.

materials.name: Starch
materials.concept: A large carbohydrate made from repeating glucose units.
materials.explanation: The n in the formula indicates that the number of repeating units can vary.
learning_goals: Interpret a repeating-unit formula.
Recognize polymers as large molecules built from repeating units.
observations: Reference entry only; it is not part of the classroom demonstration setup.

processes.name: States of matter
processes.summary: A simple particle model for solids, liquids and gases.
processes.explanation: Solids keep shape, liquids flow, gases spread out to fill the available space.
student_observations: Compare how a solid, liquid and gas are represented in the virtual classroom.
Identify which state keeps its shape and which takes the shape of its container.
model_limitations: This is a conceptual model rather than a molecular dynamics simulation.

processes.name: Melting, freezing, boiling and condensation
processes.summary: Heating and cooling can change the physical state of a substance without changing its identity.
processes.explanation: Melting turns a solid into a liquid. Freezing is the reverse. Boiling and evaporation move a substance from liquid to gas, while condensation moves a gas back to liquid.
student_observations: Identify the difference between melting and boiling.
Describe condensation as the reverse gas-to-liquid change.
model_limitations: The current app still treats this as a simplified demonstration rather than a full thermodynamic model.

processes.name: Mixtures and separation
processes.summary: Use the virtual model to discuss filtration, settling and dissolving as different classroom ideas.
processes.explanation: A mixture keeps its components in the same sample. Some mixtures can be separated physically because the components do not change into new substances.
student_observations: Compare a dissolved solution with a visible mixture.
Discuss why some materials can be separated by filtration while others cannot.
model_limitations: This entry is a teaching model, not a recipe for real laboratory work.

processes.name: Dissolution and solution formation
processes.summary: The model illustrates how an ionic solid becomes distributed through a solvent.
processes.explanation: Water molecules surround the ions at the crystal surface. The ions become dispersed through the liquid, producing a homogeneous solution.
student_observations: The visible solid amount decreases in the model.
The liquid becomes a uniform solution.
The dissolved particles are not individually visible.
model_limitations: The simulation is a simplified teaching model; its configured numerical solubility data must be reviewed before quantitative assessment.

processes.name: Saturation
processes.summary: A solution has a limit to how much solute it can contain under a specified set of conditions.
processes.explanation: A saturated solution is at the solubility limit for the chosen temperature and solvent. Adding more solute does not increase the dissolved concentration under those same conditions; extra solid can remain as a separate phase.
student_observations: Compare the meaning of dissolved material and undissolved solid.
Explain why a solution may stop becoming more concentrated.
model_limitations: The current numerical solubility curves are not approved as authoritative measured data; use this entry for the concept only.

processes.name: Conservation of mass in a closed system
processes.summary: Use a closed-container idea to show that matter is not lost when a process is only rearranging particles.
processes.explanation: In a closed system, matter is not created or destroyed during an ordinary physical change.
student_observations: Explain why a closed model is useful for classroom reasoning.
Compare a visible change with conservation of total matter.
model_limitations: This is a reasoning model only; it is not a measurement protocol.

processes.name: Food molecules and energy
processes.summary: Introduce glucose and starch as important classroom examples of biological molecules.
processes.explanation: Glucose is a small molecule that cells can use quickly. Starch is a much larger carbohydrate built from repeating units.
student_observations: Compare a small molecular formula with a repeating-unit polymer formula.
Discuss why some molecules are used by living systems as energy sources or storage molecules.
model_limitations: The app uses these only as educational examples, not as laboratory reagents.

processes.name: Photosynthesis overview
processes.summary: A safe, high-level teaching explanation of how plants use light energy to build sugar.
processes.explanation: Photosynthesis is the process by which light energy is captured and used to build carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water.
student_observations: Identify carbon dioxide and water as inputs in the overall model.
Recognize glucose as one of the products described at a high level.
model_limitations: This project does not simulate the full biochemistry or a real biological experiment.

processes.name: Cellular respiration overview
processes.summary: A safe, high-level explanation of how organisms release usable energy from food molecules.
processes.explanation: Cellular respiration is the process by which organisms extract energy from food molecules such as glucose.
student_observations: Describe glucose as an energy source in a simplified model.
Compare energy transfer with a substance-level change.
model_limitations: This is a conceptual overview only.

processes.name: Earth surface changes and carbon cycling
processes.summary: A cross-curricular concept that links gases, water and living systems.
processes.explanation: Air, carbon dioxide and water are useful reference entries when discussing the Earth system, the water cycle and carbon cycling.
student_observations: Explain why air is a mixture rather than a single pure substance.
Connect carbon dioxide to both biology and Earth science ideas.
model_limitations: The app presents this as a classroom concept only.

processes.name: Evaluate the model and choose the correct curriculum pathway
processes.summary: Treat the virtual laboratory as a scientific model and confirm the student’s official grade pathway first.
processes.explanation: A scientific model can teach ideas well while still simplifying reality. Teachers should identify what the model shows, what it leaves out and which official grade pathway the student follows before using it for planning.
student_observations: Separate a model's output from a measured result.
Identify assumptions and limitations.
Explain why the exact Senior 2 pathway is required before official Chemistry mapping.
model_limitations: The app intentionally keeps pathway selection separate from the classroom demo.

grade_experiments.title: Observing matter with a classroom solution
grade_experiments.focus: Distinguish a solid, a liquid and a simple solution using the virtual model.
student_tasks: Identify the visible state of each material.
Describe what changes when a solid becomes part of a solution.
Tell whether a sample is a pure substance or a mixture at a conceptual level.
grade_experiments.teacher_notes: Keep the activity descriptive and visual.

grade_experiments.title: Solutions, insoluble mixtures and separation ideas
grade_experiments.focus: Compare a solution with an insoluble mixture and discuss how separation ideas differ.
student_tasks: Describe the solvent and solute in the virtual model.
Explain why some materials dissolve and others do not.
Predict whether a mixture looks uniform or non-uniform.
grade_experiments.teacher_notes: Use the software to discuss concepts only.

grade_experiments.title: Saturation and closed-system reasoning
grade_experiments.focus: Introduce the idea of a solubility limit and the use of a closed-system model.
student_tasks: Explain what it means for a solution to become saturated.
Compare a visible solid with dissolved material.
Discuss why the model treats the system as simplified.
grade_experiments.teacher_notes: Let students reason from observations to ideas before giving the explanation.

grade_experiments.title: Integrated Science: matter, energy and life systems
grade_experiments.focus: Connect the classroom chemistry model to biology and Earth-system ideas.
student_tasks: Relate glucose and starch to biological energy ideas.
Describe photosynthesis and cellular respiration at a high level.
Explain why air and carbon dioxide matter in science beyond chemistry.
grade_experiments.teacher_notes: Keep the discussion conceptual and cross-curricular.

grade_experiments.title: Scientific models and pathway confirmation
grade_experiments.focus: Evaluate model limits and confirm the student’s official Senior 2 pathway before planning lessons.
student_tasks: Separate a model's output from a measured result.
Explain why the exact Senior 2 pathway is required before official Chemistry mapping.
grade_experiments.teacher_notes: Use this as a planning and evaluation lesson rather than as a promise of one fixed Senior 2 syllabus for all students.

classroom_demo.title: Water and table salt: understanding a solution
classroom_demo.purpose: Show the difference between a solid crystal and a homogeneous solution in the virtual laboratory.
app_flow: Open the project and use the default Classroom Demo setup.
Move the virtual beaker to the central work area.
Use the in-app pour/add controls to combine the two classroom-demo materials.
Select the beaker and read the Inspector observations.
Ask students to explain the roles of solvent, solute and dissolved particles.
classroom_demo.expected_learning: Students can explain that dissolving disperses particles through a solvent; the material is not simply disappearing.
assessment_prompts: Which substance is the solvent in this model?
What does a homogeneous solution mean?
How is a dissolved particle different from a visible crystal?
classroom_demo.boundary: These directions describe interaction with the virtual software only. They are not instructions for conducting a real laboratory experiment.

data_quality.summary: The current element and compound reference datasets contain fields marked unverified_reference or derived. The app must display them as reference data only and must not present them as authoritative measured values.
data_quality.element_table: All 118 elements are read-only periodic-table references. The current data source and derived electron configurations still need a complete IUPAC/NIST audit before quantitative teaching use.
data_quality.chemical_properties: Numerical properties in the chemical and compound catalogue have mixed provenance. Values marked unverified_reference must not be used for numerical assessment or as real-world specifications.
